 CLARKSBURG, W.Va. — Daylight saving time is set to end Nov. 1, with clocks falling back an hour, bringing earlier sunsets and an extra hour of sleep as the country returns to standard time.
 The time change is also an opportunity for local fire departments to encourage residents to check and update smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors.
 “We tell everybody that the best time is daylight saving time — that’s what we push for. But especially in the fall time of the year,” said Jeremy Haddix, fire chief at Nutter Fort Fire Department.
 Haddix recommends residents test their smoke alarms and replace outdated devices with detectors possessing lithium battery power for up to 10 years.
 “I’ve switched all mine in my house to the extended life alarms,” Haddix said. “You don’t have to worry about it as much, and the lithium battery stays charged. When you go to switch, go to one of them that you don’t have to mess with for 10 years.”
 Carbon monoxide detectors should also be checked and replaced, if needed, Haddix said.
 “The average lifespan of CO detectors is, I believe, 10 years. It tells you on the package. But that’s something to look at, too, is the age of it,” he said.
 According to Haddix, there is an increased risk of carbon monoxide poisoning during winter months when residents are turning on heating systems.
 “If they, for instance, would have a heat exchanger cracked in their furnace or anything that they’re burning with gas — the heat, or fuel to heat — then it’s putting off carbon monoxide,” Haddix said. “You can’t smell it or taste it, so they don’t even know what’s happening. That’s why we push so much on the carbon monoxide detectors.”
 Haddix also encourages homeowners to inspect heating furnaces for dust and debris collected over the summer to prevent house fires.
 “When they first fire it up, it gets smoky or they’ll get a haze in the house from where that dust is burning off. So it’s always a good practice to change your furnace filter or check your furnace filter before that kicks on,” he said.
 “You just want to make sure no birds have made any nests in there and just make sure that’s all clean. It is good practice.”
 Daylight saving time began as an energy-saving measure introduced in Germany during World War I and was formally recognized as a biannual event by the United States Congress through the Uniform Time Act in 1966.
 Stan Bumgardner, media editor of the West Virginia Encyclopedia Online, a project of the West Virginia Humanities Council, said daylight saving time was primarily recognized to help farmers by providing extended sunlight hours for planting and harvesting seasons.
 “As we became less agrarian, more states started adopting it just to have more daylight after work,” Bumgardner said.
 “However, when states tried to extend it year-round, parents complained that their children were having to wait for school buses and ride to school entirely in the dark. We tried this nationally in 1974, but it was eliminated after one year when all the complaints came in.”
 The campaign to make daylight saving time permanent has been debated for years, with the Sunshine Protection Act of 2025 gaining traction in Washington, which would make daylight saving time permanent across the country.
 Supporters of the legislation argue a permanent daylight saving time structure would allow more opportunity to enjoy daylight after work or school hours.
 However, some researchers and doctors warn it may disrupt individuals’ circadian rhythms, which are synchronized to a 24-hour cycle by exposure to light first thing in the morning.
 “The problem with daylight saving time is that it results in late sunrises during the winter,” said Dr. Randy Nelson, professor and chair of the Department of Neuroscience at West Virginia University.
 “Here in West Virginia, it doesn’t get light until 8:30 a.m. or later in the winter, and most of us are in school or in our workplace, so it’s easy for people not to get that early light because of the way our society’s organized,” he said.
 Nelson said the effects of a lack of exposure to light in the mornings include disruptions in sleep, hormone secretion, immune function and metabolism.
 “All these physiological processes are disrupted by not seeing bright light in the morning,” he said. “And to make it even worse, we see light in the evening when we shouldn’t see it by our devices, TVs and our computer screens and our phones and our iPads and so on.
 “It confuses our internal physiology to not function optimally.”
 Nelson agreed that not changing clocks twice a year is preferable but that standard time should be favored over permanent daylight saving time.
 “We evolved out there under standard time, right? So that would make it the best for us biologically,” he said.
 Despite the U.S. House’s July vote to approve the Sunshine Protection Act, the Senate has not yet approved the legislation, leaving the current time change schedule in place for now.
